lessons.title: Propositional Logic and Truth Tables
lessons.description: Understand logical propositions, connectives (AND, OR, NOT, XOR), and build truth tables.
lessons.formula:
NOT p: ¬p (opposite truth value)
AND: p ∧ q (true only when both true)
OR: p ∨ q (false only when both false)
XOR: p ⊕ q (true when exactly one true)
Implication: p → q (false only when p=T, q=F)
lessons.content:
A proposition is a declarative sentence that is either true or false, but not both. For example, "The sky is blue" is a proposition (it has a definite truth value), while "What time is it?" is not a proposition because it is a question. Understanding how to identify and work with propositions is the foundation of all mathematical logic and computer science reasoning.

Logical connectives allow us to build complex propositions from simpler ones. The five fundamental connectives are: NOT (negation, ¬), AND (conjunction, ∧), OR (disjunction, ∨), XOR (exclusive or, ⊕), and IMPLIES (implication, →). Each connective has a precise definition given by its truth table, which lists all possible combinations of truth values for the input propositions and the resulting truth value of the compound proposition. Memorizing these truth tables is essential.

Building a truth table for a complex expression requires listing all possible truth value combinations systematically. For n distinct variables, there are 2ⁿ rows. You evaluate the expression column by column, starting from the innermost connectives and working outward. Truth tables are used to determine whether an argument is valid, to check logical equivalences, and to simplify complex Boolean expressions in circuit design.
steps: Identify all distinct propositional variables (p, q, r, ...) in the expression
Calculate the number of rows: 2^n where n is the number of variables, and fill in all T/F combinations systematically
Create intermediate columns for sub-expressions, evaluating connectives one at a time from innermost to outermost
Evaluate the full expression for each row using the truth table definitions of each connective
Read the final column to determine the truth behavior: is it a tautology, contradiction, or contingency?

examples.title: Build a Truth Table for p ∧ (q ∨ r)
examples.text: With 3 variables there are 8 rows. Evaluate q ∨ r first: false only when both q=F and r=F. Then AND with p: p ∧ (q ∨ r) is true only when p=T AND (q ∨ r)=T. For example, when p=T, q=F, r=F: q∨r=F, so p∧(q∨r)=T∧F=F. When p=T, q=F, r=T: q∨r=T, so result=T.

examples.title: Evaluate ¬(p → q) for p=T, q=F
examples.text: First evaluate the implication p → q: it is false only when p=T and q=F. Since p=T and q=F, p → q = F. Now apply negation: ¬F = T. So ¬(p → q) = T. This is the only case where the negation of an implication is true.

lessons.tip: When building truth tables, always list combinations systematically using binary counting (TTT, TTF, TFT, TFF, FTT, FTF, FFT, FFF for 3 variables). This ensures you never miss a row and makes complex tables much easier to manage.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a proposition?
quiz.explanation: "The Earth orbits the Sun" is a declarative sentence that is definitively true, making it a proposition. The others are a command, an open equation, and a question.

quiz.q: What is p ∧ q when p is True and q is False?
quiz.explanation: AND (∧) is true only when BOTH operands are true. Since q is False, p ∧ q = False.

quiz.q: How many rows are in a truth table with 4 variables?
quiz.explanation: With n variables, a truth table has 2^n rows. For 4 variables: 2^4 = 16 rows.

quiz.q: When is the implication p → q false?
options: When p is True and q is True
When p is False and q is True
When p is True and q is False
When p is False and q is False
quiz.explanation: The implication p → q is false ONLY when the antecedent (p) is true and the consequent (q) is false. In all other cases, the implication is true.

lessons.title: Logical Equivalence and Implication
lessons.description: Prove logical equivalences using truth tables and understand tautologies, contradictions, and contingencies.
lessons.formula:
De Morgan's Laws:
¬(p ∧ q) ≡ ¬p ∨ ¬q
¬(p ∨ q) ≡ ¬p ∧ ¬q

Distributive:
p ∧ (q ∨ r) ≡ (p ∧ q) ∨ (p ∧ r)

Contrapositive:
p → q ≡ ¬q → ¬p
lessons.content:
Two propositions are logically equivalent (≡) if they have identical truth values in every possible scenario. We can verify equivalence by constructing a truth table for both expressions and confirming that their final columns match exactly. Logical equivalences allow us to transform complex expressions into simpler or more useful forms without changing their meaning, which is crucial for simplifying circuits, optimizing database queries, and writing cleaner conditions in code.

Among the most important equivalences are De Morgan's Laws, which tell us how to negate conjunctions and disjunctions: ¬(p ∧ q) ≡ ¬p ∨ ¬q and ¬(p ∨ q) ≡ ¬p ∧ ¬q. Intuitively, negating an AND gives an OR of negations, and vice versa. These laws are used extensively in set theory, Boolean algebra, and programming. Another essential equivalence is the contrapositive: p → q ≡ ¬q → ¬p, which states that an implication is logically equivalent to flipping and negating both sides.

Based on their truth tables, compound propositions fall into three categories: a tautology is always true (e.g., p ∨ ¬p), a contradiction is always false (e.g., p ∧ ¬p), and a contingency is sometimes true and sometimes false (e.g., p → q). Recognizing these patterns helps you understand the logical structure of arguments and determine whether a given statement is universally valid or depends on specific conditions.
steps: Write down both propositions side by side and identify all variables involved
Construct a single truth table with columns for each variable, each sub-expression, and both final expressions
Fill in the truth values row by row, computing each column using the definitions of the connectives
Compare the final columns of both expressions: if they match in every row, the propositions are logically equivalent
Classify each expression as a tautology (all True), contradiction (all False), or contingency (mixed)

examples.title: Verify De Morgan's Law: ¬(p ∧ q) ≡ ¬p ∨ ¬q
examples.text: Build a truth table with p, q columns. For p=T,q=T: p∧q=T, ¬(T)=F. ¬p=F, ¬q=F, F∨F=F. Match! For p=T,q=F: p∧q=F, ¬(F)=T. ¬p=F, ¬q=T, F∨T=T. Match! Checking all 4 rows confirms equivalence.

examples.title: Show p → q ≡ ¬q → ¬p (Contrapositive)
examples.text: Compare truth tables: p→q is false only when p=T,q=F. For ¬q→¬p: when p=T,q=F, ¬q=T,¬p=F, so T→F=F. Both expressions are false in exactly the same row (p=T,q=F) and true in all others. They are equivalent.

lessons.tip: De Morgan's Laws are your best friend when negating complex expressions. Remember: when you push a NOT inside parentheses, AND becomes OR and OR becomes AND. This pattern appears everywhere in programming, set theory, and circuit design.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a tautology?
quiz.explanation: p ∨ ¬p is always true: if p=T then T∨F=T; if p=F then F∨T=T. This is the Law of Excluded Middle.

quiz.q: Using De Morgan's Law, what is ¬(p ∨ q) equivalent to?
quiz.explanation: De Morgan's Law states: ¬(p ∨ q) ≡ ¬p ∧ ¬q. Negating an OR produces an AND of negations.

quiz.q: What is the contrapositive of 'If it rains, then I carry an umbrella'?
options: If I carry an umbrella, then it rains.
If it does not rain, then I do not carry an umbrella.
If I do not carry an umbrella, then it does not rain.
If it rains, then I do not carry an umbrella.
quiz.explanation: The contrapositive of p→q is ¬q→¬p. 'I carry umbrella'→¬ 'I carry umbrella' becomes 'I do NOT carry umbrella'→'it does NOT rain'.

quiz.q: A proposition that is sometimes true and sometimes false is called:
quiz.explanation: A contingency has both True and False values in its truth table, unlike a tautology (all True) or contradiction (all False).

lessons.title: Introduction to Sets and Set Operations
lessons.description: Learn set notation, union, intersection, complement, and Venn diagrams.
lessons.formula:
Union: A ∪ B (elements in A OR B)
Intersection: A ∩ B (elements in A AND B)
Complement: A' (elements NOT in A)
Difference: A - B (in A but not B)

Inclusion-Exclusion Principle:
|A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| - |A ∩ B|
lessons.content:
A set is a well-defined collection of distinct objects, called elements. Sets are fundamental to discrete mathematics and are used everywhere in computer science, from databases to algorithms. We write A = {1, 2, 3} to denote a set containing the elements 1, 2, and 3. The symbol ∈ means 'is an element of', so 2 ∈ A. Sets are unordered and contain no duplicates.

Key set operations allow us to combine and compare sets. The union (A ∪ B) contains all elements in A, B, or both. The intersection (A ∩ B) contains only elements in BOTH A and B. The complement (A') contains everything in the universal set U that is NOT in A. The difference (A - B) contains elements in A but not in B. Venn diagrams are circular representations that visually show these operations and relationships between sets.

The Inclusion-Exclusion Principle is a powerful counting formula: |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| - |A ∩ B|. It ensures we don't double-count elements that belong to both sets. This principle extends to three or more sets and is essential for solving counting problems in combinatorics, probability, and database query optimization.
steps: Define your sets clearly using roster notation {a, b, c} or set-builder notation {x | condition}
Identify the universal set U (the set of all elements under consideration)
For each operation, apply the definition: union combines, intersection keeps only common elements, complement removes
Use Venn diagrams to visualize overlapping regions and verify your answer
Apply the inclusion-exclusion principle when counting elements in unions to avoid double-counting

examples.title: Union and Intersection of Sets
examples.text: Let A = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} and B = {3, 4, 5, 6, 7}. Then A ∪ B = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7} (all elements from both sets). A ∩ B = {3, 4, 5} (only the elements they share). A - B = {1, 2} (in A but not B).

examples.title: Using the Inclusion-Exclusion Principle
examples.text: In a class of 40 students, 25 play soccer, 20 play basketball, and 10 play both. How many play at least one sport? Using inclusion-exclusion: |S ∪ B| = 25 + 20 - 10 = 35. So 35 students play at least one sport.

lessons.tip: When working with set operations, draw Venn diagrams first! They give you an intuitive picture of what's happening before you do the algebra. This is especially helpful for problems with three or more overlapping sets.

quiz.q: If A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {2, 3, 4}, what is A ∩ B?
quiz.explanation: A ∩ B is the intersection: elements in BOTH sets. Only 2 and 3 appear in both A and B.

quiz.q: The complement of A is the set of all elements that are:
options: NOT in A (relative to the universal set)
quiz.explanation: The complement A' contains every element in the universal set U that is NOT in A.

quiz.q: If |A| = 15, |B| = 12, and |A ∩ B| = 5, what is |A ∪ B|?
quiz.explanation: By the Inclusion-Exclusion Principle: |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| - |A ∩ B| = 15 + 12 - 5 = 22.

quiz.q: Which statement is true about sets?
options: The order of elements in a set matters
An element can be 'partially' in a set
quiz.explanation: Sets are unordered and contain no duplicates, so {1, 2, 3} = {3, 2, 1}. Order does not matter in sets.

lessons.title: Conditional Statements and Proof by Contraposition
lessons.description: Understand if-then statements, converse, inverse, and contrapositive, and use contrapositive proofs.
lessons.formula:
Statement: p → q
Converse: q → p
Inverse: ¬p → ¬q
Contrapositive: ¬q → ¬p

Key fact: p → q ≡ ¬q → ¬p
Only the statement and contrapositive are equivalent.
lessons.content:
A conditional statement (also called an implication) has the form 'if p, then q' (p → q), where p is the hypothesis (antecedent) and q is the conclusion (consequent). Conditional statements are the backbone of mathematical proofs, programming logic, and everyday reasoning. Saying p is sufficient for q means p → q, while saying q is necessary for p also means p → q.

From any conditional p → q, we can form three related statements. The converse (q → p) swaps the hypothesis and conclusion. The inverse (¬p → ¬q) negates both. The contrapositive (¬q → ¬p) both swaps and negates. Critically, only the original statement and its contrapositive are logically equivalent. A common logical fallacy is confusing the converse or inverse with the original statement—for example, 'If it's a dog, then it's a mammal' is true, but its converse 'If it's a mammal, then it's a dog' is false (cats are mammals too!).

Proof by contraposition is a powerful technique where instead of proving p → q directly, we prove its logically equivalent contrapositive ¬q → ¬p. This is especially useful when the negation of the conclusion gives us something concrete to work with. For example, to prove 'if n² is even, then n is even,' it's often easier to prove 'if n is odd, then n² is odd' (the contrapositive). A biconditional p ↔ q means both p → q AND q → p are true.
steps: Write the conditional statement clearly: identify the hypothesis (p) and conclusion (q)
Write the converse (q → p), inverse (¬p → ¬q), and contrapositive (¬q → ¬p)
Remember: the statement and contrapositive are equivalent; the converse and inverse are equivalent to each other
For proof by contraposition: assume ¬q and logically derive ¬p, which proves the original p → q
Check whether both directions hold to determine if you have a biconditional (p if and only if q)

examples.title: Identify Related Conditionals
examples.text:
Statement: 'If a number is divisible by 6, then it is divisible by 2.' (p → q) — TRUE.
Converse: 'If divisible by 2, then divisible by 6.' — FALSE (4 is divisible by 2 but not 6).
Contrapositive: 'If NOT divisible by 2, then NOT divisible by 6.' — TRUE (equivalent to original).

examples.title: Proof by Contraposition
examples.text: Prove: 'If 3n + 2 is odd, then n is odd.' Contrapositive: 'If n is even, then 3n + 2 is even.' Proof: If n is even, n = 2k. Then 3n + 2 = 3(2k) + 2 = 6k + 2 = 2(3k + 1), which is even. Since contrapositive is true, the original statement is true.

lessons.tip: When a direct proof seems difficult, try proof by contraposition. Negating the conclusion often gives you useful concrete information to start working with. Always ask: 'What if the conclusion were false? What would follow?'

quiz.q: What is the contrapositive of 'If it is a prime number, then it is an integer'?
options: If it is an integer, then it is a prime number.
If it is not an integer, then it is not a prime number.
If it is not a prime number, then it is not an integer.
If it is a prime number, then it is not an integer.
quiz.explanation: The contrapositive of p→q is ¬q→¬p. Negate and swap: 'If NOT an integer, then NOT a prime number.'

quiz.q: Which pairs of statements are logically equivalent?
quiz.explanation: A statement and its contrapositive are always logically equivalent (p→q ≡ ¬q→¬p).

quiz.q: The converse of 'If you study hard, then you pass the exam' is:
options: If you don't study hard, then you don't pass the exam.
If you pass the exam, then you studied hard.
If you don't pass the exam, then you didn't study hard.
Studying hard is necessary for passing.
quiz.explanation: The converse swaps hypothesis and conclusion: 'If you pass the exam (q), then you studied hard (p).' Note this is NOT equivalent to the original.

quiz.q: A biconditional p ↔ q means:
options: p implies q but q does not imply p
Both p → q and q → p are true
p and q are always the same
Neither p nor q can be true
quiz.explanation: A biconditional (p if and only if q) means both implications hold: p→q AND q→p.

lessons.title: Mathematical Induction
lessons.description: Prove statements about natural numbers using the principle of mathematical induction.
lessons.formula:
Principle of Mathematical Induction:

Step 1 (Base Case): Prove P(1) is true.
Step 2 (Inductive Step): Assume P(k) is true,
  prove P(k+1) is true.
Conclusion: P(n) is true for all n ≥ 1.
lessons.content:
Mathematical induction is one of the most powerful proof techniques in discrete mathematics. Think of it like a line of dominoes: if you push the first one (the base case) and each domino is guaranteed to knock over the next one (the inductive step), then ALL the dominoes will fall. Induction lets us prove statements that hold for infinitely many natural numbers using just two steps.

The base case verifies that the statement P(n) is true for the smallest value of n (usually n = 0 or n = 1). The inductive step assumes P(k) is true for some arbitrary k (this assumption is called the inductive hypothesis) and then proves that P(k+1) must also be true. Together, these two steps guarantee that the statement holds for every natural number. This works because the base case anchors the chain, and the inductive step extends it indefinitely.

Induction is widely used to prove formulas for sums, inequalities, divisibility properties, and properties of recursive structures. Common applications include proving that 1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n+1)/2, that n³ - n is always divisible by 6, and that 2^n > n for all natural numbers. When writing an induction proof, always clearly label the base case, state the inductive hypothesis explicitly, and show how it is used to establish P(k+1).
steps: State the proposition P(n) that you want to prove for all natural numbers n
Base Case: Substitute n = 1 (or the smallest relevant value) and verify P(1) is true
Inductive Hypothesis: Assume P(k) is true for some arbitrary natural number k ≥ 1
Inductive Step: Using the assumption P(k), algebraically or logically show that P(k+1) must be true
Conclusion: By the Principle of Mathematical Induction, P(n) is true for all natural numbers n

examples.title: Prove 1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n+1)/2
examples.text:
Base case: P(1): 1 = 1(2)/2 = 1. ✓
Inductive hypothesis: Assume 1+2+...+k = k(k+1)/2.
Inductive step: 1+2+...+k+(k+1) = k(k+1)/2 + (k+1) = (k(k+1) + 2(k+1))/2 = (k+1)(k+2)/2 = (k+1)((k+1)+1)/2. ✓
Therefore the formula holds for all n ≥ 1.

examples.title: Prove 2^n > n for all n ≥ 1
examples.text:
Base case: P(1): 2^1 = 2 > 1. ✓
Inductive hypothesis: Assume 2^k > k for some k ≥ 1.
Inductive step: 2^(k+1) = 2 · 2^k > 2 · k ≥ k + 1 (since k ≥ 1). ✓
Therefore 2^n > n for all n ≥ 1.

lessons.tip: In the inductive step, you MUST use the inductive hypothesis P(k) to prove P(k+1). If you prove P(k+1) without using P(k), you haven't done an induction proof—you've just done a direct proof. The hypothesis is the key link in the chain!

quiz.q: What is the purpose of the base case in mathematical induction?
options: To prove the statement for the largest possible value of n
To establish the starting point and anchor the proof
To show the statement is false for n = 1
quiz.explanation: The base case verifies P(1) is true, providing the foundation. Without it, the inductive chain has no starting point.

quiz.q: In the inductive step, we assume P(k) is true. What is this assumption called?
quiz.explanation: The assumption that P(k) holds for some arbitrary k is called the inductive hypothesis (IH). It is used to prove P(k+1).

quiz.q: Which of the following can be proved using mathematical induction?
options: The square root of 2 is irrational
Every continuous function has a maximum
The speed of light in a vacuum
quiz.explanation: Induction proves statements about natural numbers. The sum of the first n odd numbers equals n² is a classic inductive proof.

quiz.q: If the base case fails, what happens to the induction proof?
options: The proof still works but with a different starting point
The proof works for all n > 1 automatically
quiz.explanation: Both the base case and inductive step are required. If the base case fails, the domino chain never starts, making the proof invalid.

lessons.title: Proof by Contradiction
lessons.description: Prove statements by assuming the opposite and finding a logical contradiction.
lessons.formula:
Proof by Contradiction:

To prove P is true:
1. Assume ¬P (the negation of P).
2. Derive a contradiction (something
   that is logically impossible).
3. Conclude P must be true.
lessons.content:
Proof by contradiction (reductio ad absurdum) is a classical proof technique where we assume the opposite of what we want to prove and then show that this assumption leads to an impossible conclusion—a contradiction. Since our assumption produced something absurd, the assumption must be false, and therefore the original statement must be true. This method is especially powerful when a direct proof is difficult or when the negation of a statement gives us more concrete information to work with.

The most famous example of proof by contradiction is the proof that √2 is irrational. We start by assuming the opposite—that √2 = a/b where a and b are integers with no common factors. Squaring both sides gives 2 = a²/b², so a² = 2b². This means a² is even, so a must be even (a = 2k). Substituting: 4k² = 2b², so b² = 2k², meaning b is also even. But we assumed a and b have no common factors—both being even means they share factor 2. Contradiction! Therefore √2 is irrational.

Another celebrated application is Euclid's proof that there are infinitely many primes. Assume there are only finitely many primes: p₁, p₂, ..., pₙ. Consider N = p₁·p₂·...pₙ + 1. This N is not divisible by any of the listed primes (it leaves remainder 1 when divided by each). So either N is prime itself or has a prime factor not in our list—either way contradicts the assumption that our list was complete.
steps: Clearly state the proposition P that you want to prove
Assume the negation ¬P: suppose the opposite of P is true
Use logical reasoning, algebra, or known facts to derive consequences from ¬P
Continue deriving until you reach a contradiction—something that violates a known fact or creates an impossibility
Conclude that ¬P is false, therefore P must be true

examples.title: Prove √2 is Irrational
examples.text: Assume √2 is rational: √2 = a/b in lowest terms. Then 2 = a²/b², so a² = 2b² (a² even, so a even, a = 2k). Substituting: 4k² = 2b², so b² = 2k² (b even too). But a,b were supposed to be coprime—contradiction! Therefore √2 is irrational.

examples.title: Prove There Are Infinitely Many Primes
examples.text: Assume only finitely many primes exist: p₁, p₂, ..., pₙ. Let N = p₁·p₂·...pₙ + 1. N is not divisible by any pᵢ (remainder 1). So N is either a new prime or has a prime factor not in the list. Contradiction! Therefore infinitely many primes exist.

lessons.tip: Proof by contradiction shines when the negation of a statement is easier to work with than the statement itself. Always ask: 'What would happen if this were false?' If the answer leads to something impossible, you've found your contradiction.

quiz.q: In proof by contradiction, we start by:
options: Assuming the negation of the statement is true
quiz.explanation: Proof by contradiction begins by assuming ¬P (the opposite of what we want to prove), then deriving an impossibility.

quiz.q: The proof that √2 is irrational relies on what contradiction?
options: Both a and b are even despite being in lowest terms
quiz.explanation: The contradiction is that both a and b must be even (divisible by 2), but we assumed a/b was in lowest terms (no common factors).

quiz.q: Which of these is best suited for proof by contradiction?
options: Proving a sum formula for all n
Proving 'no integer is both even and odd'
quiz.explanation: 'No integer is both even and odd' is a negative claim. Assuming the opposite ('some integer IS both even and odd') immediately leads to a contradiction.

quiz.q: After deriving a contradiction in a proof by contradiction, you conclude:
options: The assumption was wrong, so the original statement is true
quiz.explanation: Since assuming ¬P led to an impossibility, ¬P must be false, meaning the original statement P is true.

lessons.title: Divisibility, Primes, and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
lessons.description: Understand divisibility rules, prime factorization, and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic.
lessons.formula:
Divisibility: a | b means b = a·k for integer k

Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic (FTA):
Every integer > 1 can be uniquely written
as a product of primes (up to order).

Example: 60 = 2² × 3 × 5

GCD(a,b) × LCM(a,b) = a × b
lessons.content:
Divisibility is the foundation of number theory. We say 'a divides b' (written a | b) if there exists an integer k such that b = a · k. For example, 3 | 12 because 12 = 3 · 4. Divisibility rules provide quick tests: a number is divisible by 2 if its last digit is even, by 3 if the sum of its digits is divisible by 3, by 5 if it ends in 0 or 5, and by 9 if the digit sum is divisible by 9. These rules are used constantly in simplifying fractions and checking arithmetic.

A prime number is a positive integer greater than 1 whose only divisors are 1 and itself (e.g., 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, ...). A composite number has additional divisors (e.g., 4, 6, 8, 9, 10, ...). The number 1 is neither prime nor composite. The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic (FTA) states that every integer greater than 1 can be written as a unique product of prime numbers, up to the order of the factors. For example, 84 = 2² × 3 × 7, and no other combination of primes produces 84.

The FTA is essential for computing the Greatest Common Divisor (GCD) and Least Common Multiple (LCM). Two numbers are coprime (relatively prime) if their GCD is 1. A useful relationship is GCD(a,b) × LCM(a,b) = a × b, which connects these two fundamental concepts and allows you to compute one if you know the other. Prime factorization is also the basis of the RSA encryption algorithm used to secure internet communications.
steps: To check divisibility, apply the appropriate divisibility rule (e.g., last digit for 2 and 5, digit sum for 3 and 9)
To find prime factorization, repeatedly divide by the smallest prime factor until you reach 1
Write the factorization in exponential form: e.g., 360 = 2³ × 3² × 5¹
To find GCD using prime factorization: take the minimum exponent of each common prime
To find LCM using prime factorization: take the maximum exponent of each prime that appears in either number

examples.title: Checking Coprimality
examples.text: Are 35 and 48 coprime? 35 = 5 × 7 and 48 = 2⁴ × 3. They share no common prime factors, so GCD(35, 48) = 1. Yes, 35 and 48 are coprime! Verify: GCD(35,48) × LCM(35,48) = 35 × 48 = 1680.

lessons.tip: When finding prime factorizations, always start by dividing by the smallest prime (2), then 3, then 5, etc. Keep a table of divisions to track your work. The FTA guarantees your answer is unique!

quiz.q: Which of the following is a prime number?
quiz.explanation: 29 is prime because its only divisors are 1 and 29. 15=3×5, 21=3×7, and 33=3×11 are all composite.

quiz.q: What is the prime factorization of 72?
What does the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic guarantee?
options: Every number has exactly two prime factors
Prime factorization is unique (up to order)
There are infinitely many composite numbers
quiz.explanation: The FTA states that every integer > 1 has a unique prime factorization—no matter how you factor it, you'll get the same primes with the same exponents.

quiz.q: If GCD(a, b) = 1, then a and b are:
quiz.explanation: When GCD(a,b) = 1, the numbers share no common prime factors and are called coprime or relatively prime. Neither needs to be prime itself (e.g., 35 and 48).

lessons.title: Modular Arithmetic
lessons.description: Work with clock arithmetic and congruences, the foundation of modern cryptography.
lessons.formula:
Congruence: a ≡ b (mod n) means n | (a - b)

Properties:
(a + b) mod n = ((a mod n) + (b mod n)) mod n
(a × b) mod n = ((a mod n) × (b mod n)) mod n

Fermat's Little Theorem:
If p is prime and a is not divisible by p,
then a^(p-1) ≡ 1 (mod p)
lessons.content:
Modular arithmetic is a system of arithmetic for integers where numbers 'wrap around' after reaching a value called the modulus. The most familiar example is a 12-hour clock: if it's 10 o'clock and you add 4 hours, you get 2 o'clock, not 14 o'clock. Mathematically, we write this as 10 + 4 ≡ 2 (mod 12). We say 'a is congruent to b modulo n' (a ≡ b mod n) when n divides (a - b) evenly. The set of possible remainders {0, 1, 2, ..., n-1} are called residues.

Modular arithmetic preserves addition, subtraction, and multiplication: you can reduce each operand modulo n before performing the operation, and the result will be the same. For example, (17 × 23) mod 5 = ((17 mod 5) × (23 mod 5)) mod 5 = (2 × 3) mod 5 = 6 mod 5 = 1. This property is incredibly useful for keeping numbers manageable in computations with very large values, and it is the mathematical foundation of hash functions, checksums, and cryptographic systems.

A landmark result is Fermat's Little Theorem: if p is prime and a is not divisible by p, then a^(p⁻¹) ≡ 1 (mod p). This means a^(p⁻¹) - 1 is always a multiple of p. For example, 3^6 = 729, and 729 mod 7 = 1 (since 7 × 104 = 728). This theorem is used in primality testing and is the theoretical basis for the RSA encryption algorithm that secures online communications.
steps: To compute a mod n, divide a by n and take the remainder (0 ≤ remainder < n)
For addition/subtraction mod n: reduce each number mod n, perform the operation, then reduce again
For multiplication mod n: reduce each factor mod n, multiply, then reduce the product mod n
To solve a congruence equation, test all residues 0 through n-1, or use algebraic properties
Apply Fermat's Little Theorem when working with prime moduli to simplify large exponents: a^(p-1) ≡ 1 (mod p)

examples.title: Computing 17 mod 5
examples.text: 17 ÷ 5 = 3 remainder 2, so 17 mod 5 = 2. We write 17 ≡ 2 (mod 5). Also: 17 + 8 mod 5 = 25 mod 5 = 0, because 25 is exactly divisible by 5. And 17 × 3 mod 5 = 51 mod 5 = 1 (51 = 10 × 5 + 1).

examples.title: Clock Arithmetic: What Time Is 17 Hours After 9 AM?
examples.text: Using mod 12: (9 + 17) mod 12 = 26 mod 12 = 2. So 17 hours after 9 AM is 2 AM the next day. This is why modular arithmetic is sometimes called 'clock arithmetic'—the numbers wrap around the clock face!

lessons.tip: When computing large modular expressions, always reduce modulo n at every intermediate step to keep numbers small. For example, instead of computing 7^100 directly, reduce 7^2 mod n first, then square and reduce repeatedly.

quiz.q: What is 23 mod 7?
quiz.explanation: 23 ÷ 7 = 3 remainder 2, so 23 mod 7 = 2. (Also: 23 = 3×7 + 2)

quiz.q: According to Fermat's Little Theorem, what is 3^6 mod 7?
quiz.explanation: Fermat's Little Theorem states a^(p-1) ≡ 1 (mod p). With a=3, p=7: 3^6 ≡ 1 (mod 7). Indeed, 729 = 104×7 + 1.

quiz.q: What is (14 + 11) mod 8?
quiz.explanation: 14 + 11 = 25. 25 mod 8 = 1 (since 25 = 3×8 + 1). Alternatively: (14 mod 8) + (11 mod 8) = 6 + 3 = 9, then 9 mod 8 = 1.

quiz.q: The set of residues modulo 5 is:
quiz.explanation: The residues modulo n are the remainders {0, 1, 2, ..., n-1}. For n=5, the residues are {0, 1, 2, 3, 4}.

lessons.title: Introduction to Cryptography
lessons.description: Learn the basics of encryption, from Caesar ciphers to RSA, using number theory.
lessons.formula:
Caesar Cipher:
E(x) = (x + k) mod 26
D(x) = (x - k) mod 26

RSA Encryption:
Choose primes p, q. n = p×q
φ(n) = (p-1)(q-1)
Choose e coprime to φ(n)
d = e⁻¹ mod φ(n)
Encrypt: c = m^e mod n
Decrypt: m = c^d mod n
lessons.content:
Cryptography is the science of securing communication by transforming readable messages into unreadable form. The original message is called plaintext, and the transformed message is ciphertext. The process of converting plaintext to ciphertext is encryption, and the reverse is decryption. A cipher is the algorithm that performs this transformation using a secret key. Cryptography is essential for internet security, protecting passwords, securing online banking, and enabling private communication.

The Caesar cipher is one of the oldest encryption techniques, named after Julius Caesar. It shifts each letter by a fixed number of positions in the alphabet. With a shift of 3: A→D, B→E, ..., X→A, Y→B, Z→C. Mathematically, E(x) = (x + k) mod 26 and D(x) = (x - k) mod 26, where letters are numbered 0–25. This is a symmetric cipher because the same key is used for both encryption and decryption. While trivially breakable today, the Caesar cipher illustrates the core concept of using a key to transform data.

RSA (Rivest–Shamir–Adleman) is the most widely used asymmetric (public-key) cipher. In RSA, each user has a public key (n, e) for encryption and a private key (d) for decryption. The security relies on the fact that while it's easy to multiply two large primes to get n, it's computationally infeasible to factor n back into those primes. RSA uses modular exponentiation with large numbers and depends on Euler's theorem for correctness. The math behind RSA directly builds on the number theory concepts of prime factorization and modular arithmetic.
steps: For a Caesar cipher: choose a shift value k (the key), replace each letter with the one k positions ahead
To encrypt with Caesar: E(x) = (x + k) mod 26. To decrypt: D(x) = (x - k) mod 26
For RSA key generation: choose two large primes p and q, compute n = p×q and φ(n) = (p-1)(q-1)
Choose public exponent e coprime to φ(n), compute private exponent d = e⁻¹ mod φ(n) (modular inverse)
To encrypt a message m: c = m^e mod n. To decrypt: m = c^d mod n. Only the private key holder can decrypt.

examples.title: Caesar Cipher with Shift 3
examples.text: Encrypt 'HELLO' with k=3: H(7)→K(10), E(4)→H(7), L(11)→O(14), L(11)→O(14), O(14)→R(17). Ciphertext: 'KHOOR'. To decrypt 'KHOOR': subtract 3 from each letter position. K(10)→H(7), etc. = 'HELLO'.

examples.title: Simple RSA Example
examples.text: Choose p=3, q=11. n=33, φ(n)=(3-1)(11-1)=20. Choose e=3 (coprime to 20). d = 3⁻¹ mod 20 = 7 (since 3×7=21≡1 mod 20). Public key: (33, 3). Private key: 7. Encrypt m=5: c = 5³ mod 33 = 125 mod 33 = 26. Decrypt: m = 26⁷ mod 33. Since 26² mod 33 = 676 mod 33 = 10, and 26⁴ = 10² = 100 mod 33 = 1, so 26⁷ = 26⁴ × 26³ = 1 × 26³ … working through gives m = 5. ✓

lessons.tip: The Caesar cipher has only 25 possible keys, making it trivially breakable by brute force. RSA's security comes from the enormous size of the primes (typically 2048+ bits) and the difficulty of factoring the product. The mathematics is simple, but the numbers are astronomically large.

quiz.q: In a Caesar cipher with shift 2, what does 'C' become?
quiz.explanation: C is letter 2 (0-indexed). E(x) = (2+2) mod 26 = 4, which is 'E'. A(0)→C(2), B(1)→D(3), C(2)→E(4).

quiz.q: In RSA, what makes the system secure?
options: The encryption key is very long
It is hard to factor n back into the original primes p and q
quiz.explanation: RSA's security relies on the computational difficulty of factoring a large product n = p×q into its prime factors, which is easy to compute but extremely hard to reverse.

quiz.q: What is the difference between symmetric and asymmetric encryption?
options: Symmetric uses numbers, asymmetric uses letters
Symmetric uses the same key for encryption and decryption; asymmetric uses different keys
quiz.explanation: Symmetric encryption (like Caesar cipher) uses one shared key for both operations. Asymmetric (like RSA) uses a public key for encryption and a different private key for decryption.

quiz.q: In RSA, the public key consists of:
quiz.explanation: The RSA public key is (n, e), where n = p×q is the modulus and e is the public exponent. The private key is d, and φ(n) must be kept secret.

lessons.title: Introduction to Graph Theory
lessons.description: Understand vertices, edges, paths, and different types of graphs.
lessons.formula:
Degree of vertex: number of edges incident to it

Handshaking Lemma:
Sum of all degrees = 2 × (number of edges)

Complete graph K_n:
Number of edges = n(n-1)/2
lessons.content:
A graph G = (V, E) consists of a set of vertices (also called nodes) V and a set of edges E connecting pairs of vertices. Graphs are used to model countless real-world systems: social networks (people as vertices, friendships as edges), transportation networks (cities as vertices, roads as edges), computer networks, molecular structures, and dependencies in scheduling. Understanding graph theory is essential for computer science because trees, networks, and relationships are everywhere.

The degree of a vertex is the number of edges connected to it. The Handshaking Lemma states that the sum of all vertex degrees equals twice the number of edges. This means the number of odd-degree vertices must always be even! Graphs can be directed (edges have arrows, like one-way streets) or undirected (edges have no direction). They can also be weighted (edges have numerical values, like distances or costs) or unweighted. A complete graph K_n connects every vertex to every other vertex and has n(n-1)/2 edges.

Important concepts include paths (sequences of vertices connected by edges with no repeats) and cycles (paths that return to the starting vertex). An Euler path visits every edge exactly once and exists if the graph has exactly 0 or 2 odd-degree vertices. A Hamiltonian path visits every vertex exactly once—determining whether one exists is computationally hard (NP-complete). These concepts connect to practical problems like route planning, circuit board design, and DNA sequencing.
steps: Identify the vertices (nodes) and edges (connections) in your graph
Determine if the graph is directed (arrows), undirected (no arrows), weighted (numbers on edges), or unweighted
Calculate the degree of each vertex (count edges) and verify the Handshaking Lemma
Check for paths (vertex sequences without repetition) and cycles (paths returning to start)
Apply Euler/Hamiltonian criteria: Euler path exists if 0 or 2 odd-degree vertices; Hamiltonian paths require exhaustive search

examples.title: Degrees and the Handshaking Lemma
examples.text: Graph with 4 vertices: A-B, B-C, C-D, D-A, A-C. Degrees: deg(A)=3, deg(B)=2, deg(C)=3, deg(D)=2. Sum = 3+2+3+2 = 10 = 2×5 edges. ✓ Handshaking Lemma holds! Odd-degree vertices: A and C (2 of them—always even!).

examples.title: Complete Graph K_5
examples.text: K_5 has 5 vertices with every pair connected. Number of edges = 5(5-1)/2 = 10. Each vertex has degree 4. Sum of degrees = 5×4 = 20 = 2×10. ✓ K_5 cannot be drawn on paper without crossing edges—it's non-planar!

lessons.tip: The Handshaking Lemma is a great quick-check: count all degrees and divide by 2—you should get the number of edges. If you don't, you miscounted! Also, the number of odd-degree vertices is always even.

quiz.q: The Handshaking Lemma states that the sum of all vertex degrees equals:
quiz.explanation: Every edge contributes 1 to the degree of two vertices, so sum of degrees = 2 × |E|.

quiz.q: How many edges does a complete graph K_6 have?
quiz.explanation: K_n has n(n-1)/2 edges. K_6 = 6×5/2 = 15 edges.

quiz.q: An Euler path visits every _____ exactly once.
quiz.explanation: An Euler path traverses every edge exactly once. A Hamiltonian path visits every vertex exactly once.

quiz.q: A graph where edges have arrows indicating direction is called:
quiz.explanation: A directed graph (digraph) has edges with direction (arrows), representing one-way relationships like one-way streets or follow relationships.

lessons.title: Graph Representations: Adjacency Matrix and List
lessons.description: Represent graphs using adjacency matrices and adjacency lists.
lessons.formula:
Adjacency Matrix A[i][j]:
  = 1 if edge from i to j (unweighted)
  = weight if edge exists (weighted)
  = ∞ (or 0) if no edge

Space Complexity:
  Matrix: O(V²)
  List: O(V + E)

Use matrix for dense graphs,
use list for sparse graphs.
lessons.content:
To work with graphs in computer programs, we need a way to represent them in memory. The two most common representations are the adjacency matrix and the adjacency list. Each has different trade-offs in terms of space and time efficiency, and choosing the right one depends on the structure of your graph and the operations you need to perform.

An adjacency matrix is a V×V (vertices by vertices) 2D array where A[i][j] = 1 if there is an edge from vertex i to vertex j (for unweighted graphs) or A[i][j] = weight (for weighted graphs). If no edge exists, A[i][j] = 0 or ∞. Checking whether an edge exists between two specific vertices takes O(1) time—just look up the matrix entry. However, finding all neighbors of a vertex requires scanning the entire row, taking O(V) time, and the matrix always uses O(V²) space regardless of how many edges exist.

An adjacency list stores, for each vertex, a list (or array) of its neighbors. This uses O(V + E) space—proportional to the actual number of edges, making it very efficient for sparse graphs (graphs where E is much less than V²). Finding all neighbors takes O(degree) time. For dense graphs (many edges), the adjacency matrix may be more convenient. In practice, most real-world graphs (social networks, web links, road networks) are sparse, making the adjacency list the preferred representation.
steps: List all vertices and number them 0 through V-1 for indexing
For adjacency matrix: create a V×V table, set A[i][j] to 1 (or weight) for each edge (i,j), 0 otherwise
For adjacency list: create an array of V lists, for each vertex add all its neighbors to its list
Choose the representation based on graph density: matrix for dense, list for sparse
Consider the operations needed: matrix for fast edge lookup (O(1)), list for efficient neighbor iteration (O(degree))

examples.title: Adjacency Matrix for a Triangle (3 vertices)
examples.text:
Vertices: 0, 1, 2. Edges: 0-1, 1-2, 2-0.
Adjacency Matrix:
    0  1  2
0 [ 0  1  1 ]
1 [ 1  0  1 ]
2 [ 1  1  0 ]
Space used: 3×3 = 9 entries. Symmetric for undirected graph.

examples.title: Adjacency List for the Same Triangle
examples.text:
Adjacency List:
0 → [1, 2]
1 → [0, 2]
2 → [0, 1]
Space used: 3 vertices + 6 neighbor entries = O(V+E) = O(6). Finding neighbors of vertex 0: just read list [1, 2] in O(degree) time.

lessons.tip: For real-world graphs (social networks, web graphs, transportation networks), adjacency lists are almost always better because these graphs are sparse. Only use adjacency matrices for small, dense graphs or when you need constant-time edge existence checks.

quiz.q: What is the space complexity of an adjacency matrix for a graph with V vertices?
quiz.explanation: An adjacency matrix is a V×V 2D array, so it uses O(V²) space regardless of the number of edges.

quiz.q: Which representation is better for a sparse graph with 10,000 vertices but only 20,000 edges?
quiz.explanation: The adjacency list uses O(V+E) = O(30,000) space, while the matrix uses O(V²) = O(100,000,000). The list is far more efficient for sparse graphs.

quiz.q: Checking if a specific edge (u, v) exists takes O(1) time in:
quiz.explanation: In an adjacency matrix, just look up A[u][v] in constant time. In a list, you need to scan the neighbor list of u, taking O(degree) time.

quiz.q: A graph with 1000 vertices and ~500,000 edges is considered:
quiz.explanation: The maximum possible edges = 1000×999/2 ≈ 500,000. Having ~500,000 edges means the graph is nearly complete—very dense.

lessons.title: Graph Traversal: BFS and DFS
lessons.description: Explore graphs systematically using Breadth-First Search and Depth-First Search.
lessons.formula:
BFS (Breadth-First Search):
  Data structure: Queue (FIFO)
  Explores level by level
  Time: O(V + E)
  Finds shortest path (unweighted)

DFS (Depth-First Search):
  Data structure: Stack (LIFO) or recursion
  Goes as deep as possible first
  Time: O(V + E)
  Useful for: topological sort, cycle detection
lessons.content:
Graph traversal is the process of systematically visiting all vertices in a graph. The two fundamental traversal algorithms are Breadth-First Search (BFS) and Depth-First Search (DFS). Both visit every reachable vertex exactly once in O(V + E) time, but they explore the graph in very different orders. These algorithms are the backbone of countless graph applications including shortest path finding, connectivity checking, cycle detection, and topological sorting.

BFS explores the graph level by level, like ripples in a pond. Starting from a source vertex, it visits all neighbors first, then all neighbors' neighbors, and so on. BFS uses a queue (First-In, First-Out) data structure. The key property of BFS is that it finds the shortest path (in terms of number of edges) from the source to all other vertices in an unweighted graph. BFS is used in social network friend recommendations, web crawling, and finding the minimum number of moves in puzzles.

DFS dives as deep as possible along each branch before backtracking, like exploring a maze by always going forward until hitting a dead end. DFS uses a stack (Last-In, First-Out) or, more commonly, recursion. DFS is particularly useful for detecting cycles in a graph, finding connected components, performing topological sorting of a directed acyclic graph, and solving maze problems. The order of DFS depends on how neighbors are listed, but all reachable vertices are visited.
steps: Start at a source vertex, mark it as visited, and add it to the queue (BFS) or stack (DFS)
While the queue/stack is not empty, remove the next vertex and process it
For BFS: add all unvisited neighbors to the back of the queue (FIFO order)
For DFS: push all unvisited neighbors onto the top of the stack (LIFO order), or recursively visit each unvisited neighbor
Repeat until all reachable vertices are visited. Track parent pointers if you need to reconstruct paths.

examples.title: Trace BFS on a Small Graph
examples.text:
Graph: 0-1, 0-2, 1-3, 2-3, 3-4. Start at 0.
Queue: [0] → visit 0, neighbors {1,2} → Queue: [1, 2]
Visit 1, neighbors {3} → Queue: [2, 3]
Visit 2, neighbor {3} already queued → Queue: [3]
Visit 3, neighbors {4} → Queue: [4]
Visit 4, no unvisited neighbors. Queue empty.
BFS order: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. Shortest path 0→4 = 0→3→4 (3 edges).

examples.title: Trace DFS on the Same Graph
examples.text:
Graph: 0-1, 0-2, 1-3, 2-3, 3-4. Start at 0.
Visit 0, explore neighbor 1 → Visit 1, explore neighbor 3 → Visit 3, explore neighbor 4 → Visit 4 (dead end, backtrack)
Back at 3, neighbor 2 unvisited → Visit 2 (neighbors 0,3 both visited, backtrack)
Back at 3, done. Back at 1, done. Back at 0, done.
DFS order: 0, 1, 3, 4, 2. Note: DFS reaches vertex 4 before vertex 2!

lessons.tip: BFS uses a QUEUE (FIFO—think 'wave spreading outward') and finds shortest paths. DFS uses a STACK or RECURSION (LIFO—think 'going deep first') and is better for exploring structure like cycles and connectivity. Keep these data structure differences straight!

quiz.q: Which data structure does BFS use?
quiz.explanation: BFS uses a Queue (FIFO) to explore vertices level by level, ensuring all neighbors at distance d are visited before distance d+1.

quiz.q: Which traversal is guaranteed to find the shortest path in an unweighted graph?
quiz.explanation: BFS explores vertices in order of their distance from the source, so the first time it reaches a vertex, it's via the shortest path.

quiz.q: DFS is particularly useful for:
quiz.explanation: DFS's depth-first nature makes it ideal for topological sorting (process nodes in dependency order) and detecting cycles (finding back edges).

quiz.q: What is the time complexity of both BFS and DFS?
quiz.explanation: Both BFS and DFS visit each vertex once and examine each edge once (using adjacency list), giving O(V + E) time complexity.

lessons.title: Dijkstra's Shortest Path Algorithm
lessons.description: Find the shortest path between nodes in a weighted graph using Dijkstra's algorithm.
lessons.formula:
Dijkstra's Algorithm:
1. dist[start] = 0, dist[others] = ∞
2. Visit unvisited vertex with smallest dist
3. For each neighbor: dist[nbr] = min(dist[nbr],
   dist[current] + weight(current, nbr))
4. Repeat until all visited or target found

Time: O(V²) naive,
O((V+E) log V) with priority queue
lessons.content:
Dijkstra's algorithm finds the shortest path from a single source vertex to all other vertices in a weighted graph with non-negative edge weights. It is one of the most important and widely-used algorithms in computer science, powering GPS navigation systems, network routing protocols (OSPF), game AI pathfinding, and logistics optimization. Dijkstra's algorithm is a greedy algorithm: at each step, it picks the unvisited vertex with the smallest known distance and 'locks in' that distance as optimal.

The algorithm maintains a distance table where dist[v] stores the shortest known distance from the source to vertex v. Initially, dist[start] = 0 and dist[others] = ∞. At each iteration, we pick the unvisited vertex with the smallest dist value and relax its edges: for each neighbor, we check if going through the current vertex gives a shorter path than previously known. If dist[current] + weight < dist[neighbor], we update dist[neighbor]. This relaxation step is the heart of the algorithm.

A critical limitation: Dijkstra's algorithm does not work with negative edge weights. If a graph has negative weights, use the Bellman-Ford algorithm instead. Using a priority queue (min-heap) improves the time complexity from O(V²) to O((V+E) log V) by efficiently selecting the next vertex. For dense graphs, a simple array scan may be faster due to lower constant factors. The algorithm can also be stopped early once the target vertex is visited, saving unnecessary computation.
steps: Initialize distances: set dist[source] = 0 and dist[v] = ∞ for all other vertices. Mark all vertices as unvisited.
Select the unvisited vertex u with the smallest distance value dist[u]. If all remaining are ∞, stop.
For each unvisited neighbor v of u: compute the candidate distance dist[u] + weight(u,v). If it's smaller than dist[v], update dist[v] = dist[u] + weight(u,v).
Mark vertex u as visited. A visited vertex's distance is now finalized and will never change.
Repeat steps 2–4 until all vertices are visited or the target is reached. The dist array now contains the shortest path distances.

examples.title: Trace Dijkstra on a 4-Vertex Graph
Why Dijkstra Fails with Negative Weights
examples.text: Graph: A→B(3), B→C(2), A→C(6). Dijkstra picks A→C directly (dist=6) first, but A→B(3)+B→C(2)=5 is shorter. Now add A→C(-5). If we visit A first, lock C at -5, then find A→B(3)+B→C(2)=5. We'd never update C because it's 'visited'. But A→C(-5)=-5 < 5, which is correct. Dijkstra's greedy locking-in fails with negative edges.

lessons.tip: When tracing Dijkstra by hand, keep a table showing: current vertex, distances to all vertices after relaxation, and which vertices are visited. Update the table row by row. The key insight is: once a vertex is visited, its distance is final.

quiz.q: Dijkstra's algorithm does NOT work correctly when the graph has:
quiz.explanation: Dijkstra assumes non-negative weights. With negative weights, the greedy choice of 'locking in' the nearest unvisited vertex may give a suboptimal result. Use Bellman-Ford instead.

quiz.q: The 'relaxation' step in Dijkstra's checks whether:
options: Going through the current vertex gives a shorter path to a neighbor
quiz.explanation: Relaxation checks: is dist[current] + weight(current, neighbor) < dist[neighbor]? If yes, update dist[neighbor] to the shorter path.

quiz.q: Using a priority queue improves Dijkstra's time complexity to:
quiz.explanation: A min-heap priority queue allows O(log V) extraction of the minimum-distance vertex, improving from O(V²) to O((V+E) log V).

quiz.q: Dijkstra's algorithm is classified as a _____ algorithm.
quiz.explanation: Dijkstra's is greedy because at each step it makes the locally optimal choice (visit the vertex with smallest current distance), which leads to the globally optimal solution.

lessons.title: Minimum Spanning Trees: Prim's and Kruskal's Algorithms
lessons.description: Find the minimum cost to connect all vertices using MST algorithms.
lessons.formula:
MST Properties:
- Connects all vertices with minimum total
  edge weight
- Has exactly V - 1 edges
- Contains no cycles

Prim's: Grow tree from start vertex,
  add cheapest connecting edge each step.

Kruskal's: Sort all edges by weight,
  add cheapest edge that creates no cycle
  (use Union-Find to detect cycles).
lessons.content:
A Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) of a connected, undirected, weighted graph is a spanning tree (a subgraph that connects all vertices) with the minimum possible total edge weight. An MST always has exactly V-1 edges and contains no cycles. MSTs have numerous applications: laying cable to connect buildings at minimum cost, designing efficient network infrastructure, clustering data points, and approximating the Traveling Salesman Problem. There may be multiple valid MSTs for a graph (all with the same minimum total weight).

Prim's algorithm grows the MST from a starting vertex by repeatedly adding the cheapest edge that connects a vertex in the growing tree to a vertex not yet in the tree. Starting from any vertex, it maintains a set of 'in-tree' vertices and at each step adds the minimum-weight edge crossing the cut between in-tree and out-of-tree vertices. Using a priority queue, Prim's runs in O((V+E) log V) time, making it very efficient for dense graphs. It is essentially Dijkstra's algorithm with edge weight instead of path distance.

Kruskal's algorithm takes a different approach: it sorts ALL edges by weight and adds them one by one to the growing forest, skipping any edge that would create a cycle. Cycle detection is done efficiently using the Union-Find (Disjoint Set) data structure, which tracks which vertices are connected. Kruskal's runs in O(E log E) time (dominated by sorting edges). It is particularly efficient for sparse graphs and has the advantage of being easy to implement. Both algorithms produce a valid MST—the choice depends on graph density.
steps: Prim's: Start with any vertex in the MST set. Add all its edges to a priority queue (min-heap).
Prim's: Extract the minimum-weight edge from the queue. If it connects to an unvisited vertex, add it to the MST and add the new vertex's edges to the queue.
Prim's: Repeat until V-1 edges are selected or all vertices are in the MST.
Kruskal's: Sort all edges by weight in ascending order. Initialize Union-Find with each vertex in its own set.
Kruskal's: For each edge in order: if its endpoints are in different sets (no cycle), add it to the MST and union the sets. Stop after V-1 edges.

examples.title: Trace Prim's Algorithm
Trace Kruskal's Algorithm

lessons.tip: Both Prim's and Kruskal's always produce a valid MST with the same minimum total weight (though the actual edges may differ). Choose Prim's for dense graphs (many edges relative to vertices) and Kruskal's for sparse graphs (few edges). Union-Find makes Kruskal's very efficient.

quiz.q: How many edges does a Minimum Spanning Tree have for a graph with V vertices?
quiz.explanation: A spanning tree connects all V vertices with exactly V-1 edges. Adding any more would create a cycle; removing any would disconnect the graph.

quiz.q: Kruskal's algorithm uses which data structure to detect cycles?
quiz.explanation: Union-Find tracks which vertices belong to the same connected component. If both endpoints of an edge are already in the same set, adding it would create a cycle.

quiz.q: Both Prim's and Kruskal's algorithms are classified as:
quiz.explanation: Both are greedy: Prim's always picks the cheapest edge crossing the cut, Kruskal's always picks the cheapest edge that doesn't form a cycle.

quiz.q: Which algorithm is better suited for dense graphs?
options: Both are equally efficient for dense graphs
quiz.explanation: Prim's with priority queue runs in O((V+E)log V). For dense graphs where E ≈ V², this is better than Kruskal's O(E log E) which is dominated by sorting many edges.

lessons.title: Network Flow and Connectivity
lessons.description: Understand maximum flow, minimum cut, and graph connectivity concepts.
lessons.formula:
Max-Flow Min-Cut Theorem:
Maximum flow = Minimum cut capacity

Ford-Fulkerson Method:
1. Find an augmenting path in the
   residual graph (path from s to t)
2. Push as much flow as possible
   along this path (bottleneck capacity)
3. Update residual graph
4. Repeat until no augmenting path exists

k-Connected: graph stays connected after
removing any k-1 vertices.
lessons.content:
A flow network is a directed graph where each edge has a capacity (maximum amount of flow it can carry) and edges carry flow from a source vertex s to a sink vertex t. The goal of the maximum flow problem is to find the greatest possible total flow from s to t without exceeding any edge capacity. Flow networks model real-world systems: water pipes (capacity = pipe size, flow = water), transportation (capacity = road capacity, flow = traffic), communication networks (capacity = bandwidth, flow = data), and supply chain logistics.

The Max-Flow Min-Cut Theorem is one of the most elegant results in combinatorial optimization. It states that the maximum amount of flow from s to t equals the capacity of the minimum cut—the smallest total capacity of edges whose removal would disconnect s from t. This theorem connects two seemingly different problems (maximizing flow and minimizing cut) and provides a way to verify optimality. The Ford-Fulkerson method finds maximum flow by repeatedly discovering augmenting paths in the residual graph (which shows remaining capacity and allows flow to be 'pushed back').

Graph connectivity measures how robust a graph is. A graph is k-connected if it remains connected after removing any k-1 vertices. For example, a ring of 4 vertices is 2-connected (removing any single vertex leaves a connected path). Connectivity has practical implications: a 2-connected road network has no single point of failure, and a k-connected communication network tolerates up to k-1 node failures. Menger's Theorem connects k-connectivity to the number of vertex-disjoint paths between any two vertices.
steps: Set up the flow network: identify source s, sink t, edge capacities, and initialize all flows to 0.
Build the residual graph: for each edge with flow f and capacity c, the residual capacity is c-f (forward) and f (backward for flow reduction).
Find an augmenting path: any path from s to t in the residual graph using edges with positive residual capacity.
Push flow along the augmenting path: the amount pushed equals the minimum residual capacity along the path (the bottleneck).
Update the residual graph and repeat steps 3-4 until no augmenting path exists. The total flow is the maximum flow, and the minimum cut equals it.

examples.title: Maximum Flow in a Simple Network
examples.text:
Source S → A(cap 10) → T(cap 8), S → B(cap 8) → T(cap 10), A → B(cap 5).
Path 1: S→A→T, bottleneck = min(10,8) = 8. Flow = 8.
Residual: S→A(2), A→T(0, backward 8), S→B(8), B→T(10), A→B(5).
Path 2: S→B→T, bottleneck = min(8,10) = 8. Flow = 8. Total = 16.
Path 3: S→A→B→T, bottleneck = min(2,5,10-8=2) = 2. Total = 18.
No more augmenting paths. Max flow = 18.

examples.title: Minimum Cut Verification
examples.text:
Cut {S,A} from {B,T}: edges crossing = A→T(8) + S→B(8) = 16. But max flow = 18 > 16, so this is NOT the min cut.
Cut {S} from {A,B,T}: edges = S→A(10) + S→B(8) = 18. This matches max flow!
By Max-Flow Min-Cut Theorem, this IS the minimum cut with capacity 18, confirming max flow = 18.

lessons.tip: When solving max-flow problems by hand, always update the residual graph after each augmenting path. Look for augmenting paths that use backward edges (flow reduction) too—these can increase total flow even when all forward paths are saturated!

quiz.q: The Max-Flow Min-Cut Theorem states that:
options: Maximum flow is always less than minimum cut
Maximum flow equals minimum cut capacity
Maximum flow is unrelated to cuts
quiz.explanation: The theorem guarantees that the maximum possible flow from source to sink exactly equals the capacity of the minimum cut separating them.

quiz.q: An augmenting path is:
options: The longest path in the graph
A path in the residual graph from source to sink with positive residual capacity
A path that creates a cycle
The path with the maximum total capacity
quiz.explanation: An augmenting path goes from s to t in the residual graph using edges with remaining capacity. The bottleneck (minimum residual) determines how much flow to push.

quiz.q: A 3-connected graph can withstand the removal of how many vertices and still be connected?
quiz.explanation: A k-connected graph remains connected after removing any k-1 vertices. So 3-connected means it survives removal of up to 2 vertices.

quiz.q: The residual graph includes backward edges because:
options: They allow flow to be redirected (reduced) to find better overall flow
They represent new edges in the network
quiz.explanation: Backward edges in the residual graph represent the ability to 'undo' or redirect previously assigned flow, allowing the algorithm to find more efficient overall flow distributions.
